description: For this challenge we want to build something genuinely creative, insanely well designed and backed by solid code and smart logic. We’re keeping things fun and focusing on creating a project that truly stands out globally.
summary:
We developed FieldShift UZ, a lightweight, mobile-friendly Progressive Web App (PWA) designed to help farmers in Uzbekistan adapt to climate change using NASA Earth observation data.

Farmers simply tap their field on an interactive map to get instant, plain-language answers to four critical questions: land suitability, historical rainfall and cloud trends, 20 year vegetation health, and tailored crop recommendations. By combining NASA datasets (MODIS, GPM, SMAP, POWER) and SoilGrids with FAO EcoCrop standards, our engine clearly categorizes crops as Recommended, Risky, or Not Suitable based on local soil salinity and climate. Additionally, an interactive Climate Scenario Simulator lets users test future heatwaves (+1°C/+2°C) and rainfall drops (-15%) in real time, while Open-Meteo integration provides 10 day irrigation alerts.

FieldShift UZ is vital because it bridges the gap between complex space science and local agriculture empowering farmers to conserve scarce water, prevent crop failure, and secure food production.
details:
What we built and how it works We built FieldShift UZ, a simple mobile web app (PWA) made for farmers and agronomists in Uzbekistan. Instead of forcing farmers to read complicated satellite charts, our app lets them tap their field on a map and get straight answers to four practical questions: Is this land good for farming? What do the rain and cloud patterns look like? Which crops will grow well here, and which ones are too risky? Finally, how has this land changed over the last five years?

Under the hood, we match local soil and weather data against FAO EcoCrop standards. The app sorts crops into three clear groups—Recommended, Risky, or Not Suitable—and explains the reason in plain Uzbek, Russian, or English. For example, it warns against planting rice in dry regions or tells a farmer when salty soil might hurt their wheat yield. We also added an interactive climate slider (+1°C, +2°C heat, or -15% rain) so users can see how future climate shifts would change their crop choices in real time.

Why it matters Across Uzbekistan, water shortages and salty soil are forcing farmers to guess what to plant, often costing them their harvest. By turning open space data into clear "plant this, avoid that" advice on any phone—without needing to download a heavy app—we want to help local farmers save water and protect their income.

Tools and data we used We built the whole web app using Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet for the interactive map, and Recharts for the data graphs. For historical and current land data, we used NASA datasets—MODIS (land cover, NDVI,GPP/NPP, clouds), GPM IMERG (rainfall), SMAP (soil moisture), NASA POWER, and SRTM—alongside SoilGrids for soil pH and salinity.

What makes our approach different One thing we cared a lot about was being honest with the science. NASA satellites show us what happened in the past and what is happening now, not whether it will rain next Tuesday. So, we paired NASA's historical data with the free Open-Meteo API to give farmers real 10-day irrigation warnings. Also, knowing that rural internet can be slow, we pre-cached data for five key regions—Tashkent, Fergana, Karakalpakstan, Surkhandarya,and Samarkand—so the app loads fast even out in the field.
